title: Readiness Posture: An Overview
lede: Kronos states plainly what is designed, what is simulated, and what remains to be demonstrated in hardware.
body: A defense customer cannot plan around a promise that outruns the evidence. Kronos treats readiness as a claim that must be earned gate by gate, and it publishes the gates rather than the hype. Both machines — the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) — are today design and simulation studies. No hardware net-gain result has been produced, and none is claimed before the first-of-a-kind (FOAK) breeder produces first tritium, targeted for approximately 2030 with construction beginning Q2 2027.

This category documents three things a serious counterpart needs: the honest gates and timeline that separate design from demonstration; the standards and compliance frameworks Kronos designs to; and the responsible dual-use posture that keeps civilian energy primary while making conservative, public-only claims about defense value.
Breeder (Hyperion): D-T spherical tokamak, simulated Q_sci 3.424, fusion power 88.7 MW, plasma current 9.86 MA, peak field 16.84 T, negative triangularity delta -0.30.
Burner (Aegis / MetroVolt): D-3He tandem-mirror generator, 26.49 T plug, 17 T throat, neutron fraction 5.44%, direct energy conversion.
Tritium breeding ratio (TBR) is treated as a design lever across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8 — not a settled result.
Every figure above comes from the public design basis. Where a number is a target, a lever, or a simulation output rather than a measurement, this library says so.

title: Design-Stage vs Demonstrated
lede: A precise line between what exists as a validated design and what has been shown in operating hardware.
body: Confidence in a design comes from physics that closes on paper and in simulation, cross-checked against experiments others have run. Confidence in a demonstrated capability comes from the specific machine doing the specific thing. These are not interchangeable, and conflating them is the most common way fusion programs lose credibility.
What is design-stage at Kronos today
The breeder's plasma scenario (Q_sci 3.424, 88.7 MW, 9.86 MA) — a simulation result, not a shot on a machine.
The burner's tandem-mirror confinement at a 26.49 T plug — a design point, gated on an open plug-density requirement.
Tritium breeding at ratios of 1.1 / 1.5 / 1.8 — modeled as a lever, with local-vs-net reconciliation still open.
Direct energy conversion efficiency in the burner — engineering design, not a delivered subsystem.
What is demonstrated — by the field, not by us

D-T fusion power, spherical-tokamak operation, high-field REBCO magnets, and tritium handling all have real experimental heritage in the broader community. Kronos builds on that heritage; it does not claim that heritage as its own hardware result. The distinction matters for a defense planner who must know which risks are retired and which are still live.
When a page in this library states a number, check the verb: simulated, designed, targeted, and measured are not synonyms, and we do not treat them as such.

title: Technology Readiness Levels
lede: The nine-level TRL scale, and an honest placement of the Kronos machines within it.
body: Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) are a 1-to-9 scale, widely used across defense acquisition, for describing how mature a technology is — from basic principles observed (TRL 1) through a system proven in operational use (TRL 9). The scale is deliberately coarse; its value is a common language, not false precision.
Core plasma physics and confinement concepts draw on decades of community research (higher TRL for the concepts themselves).
The specific Kronos breeder and burner integrated designs sit in the research-and-feasibility band (TRL 1-3) as design & simulation studies.
Component technologies vary: REBCO high-field magnets and tritium handling have more experimental maturity than the integrated Kronos systems that use them.

A TRL is assigned to a specific technology in a specific application, not to a field. It would be inaccurate to inherit the field's maturity for an integrated machine that has not been built. Construction of the FOAK breeder begins Q2 2027; first tritium is targeted for approximately 2030. Only operating hardware moves the integrated system up the scale, and Kronos will report that movement when it happens, not before.
TRL is paired with manufacturing and integration readiness on adjacent pages, because a plant is only as ready as the least ready of the three.

title: Manufacturing Readiness
lede: Manufacturing Readiness Levels ask a separate question: can the design actually be built, repeatably and to spec.
body: Design readiness is not build readiness

A technology can be sound and still be unmanufacturable at rate. Manufacturing Readiness Levels (MRLs) run a parallel 1-to-10 scale that asks whether the materials, tooling, workforce, and quality systems exist to produce a design consistently. For a defense program that will need replicated units, MRL is as decisive as TRL.
High-field REBCO magnets require specialty conductor whose supply chain is maturing but not yet at fleet volume.
Nuclear-grade fabrication (welding, inspection, traceability) is well established in industry but must be qualified for these specific components.
The FOAK breeder is, by definition, a first article — its purpose includes proving the manufacturing route, not assuming it.

The build sequence is designed so manufacturing learning is captured: the first-of-a-kind (FOAK) unit surfaces the hard fabrication problems, the next-of-a-kind (NOAK) applies the fixes, and the balance-of-kind (BOAK) fleet benefits from a stabilized process. Manufacturing readiness therefore rises across units by design, and none of it is assumed to be solved on paper.

title: Integration Readiness
lede: Integration Readiness Levels measure whether subsystems that each work alone will work together as a plant.
body: The interfaces are where systems fail

Most complex-system failures live at interfaces, not inside boxes. Integration Readiness Levels (IRLs) grade how well two subsystems have been shown to interoperate — from an interface merely identified through interfaces verified and validated under mission conditions. A fusion plant has many such interfaces: plasma to magnets, magnets to cryogenics, blanket to fuel cycle, control system to everything.
The breeder fuel cycle: tritium bred in the blanket must be recovered and returned faster than it decays or is lost — the local-vs-net TBR question is fundamentally an integration question.
The burner plug: sustaining a 26.49 T plug at the required plasma density couples magnet, heating, and confinement subsystems, and the plug-density requirement remains an open gate.
Real-time plasma control couples sensing, computation, and actuation on microsecond timescales.

A predictive digital twin lets integration be rehearsed before hardware exists, so interface assumptions are tested in simulation first. This raises integration confidence but does not substitute for it: an integrated hardware demonstration is the only thing that closes an IRL at the top of the scale.

title: Catalog of Honest Gates
lede: A single list of the open questions that stand between the present design and a demonstrated capability.
body: An honest gate is a specific, falsifiable question whose answer is not yet in hand and which must be answered before a claim can be upgraded. Kronos publishes its gates so that partners can judge the program on evidence rather than narrative. The list below is deliberately conservative and is maintained as questions are opened or retired.
A gate closes only with evidence appropriate to its claim: a hardware claim needs hardware, a simulation claim needs reproducible code and benchmarks.
Closing a gate never opens a stronger claim than the evidence supports — a met simulation gate does not become a hardware result.
Retired gates stay on record so the program's history is auditable.

Two gates dominate the technical risk today. First, the breeder must produce net tritium once realistic three-dimensional geometry, ports, and structure are accounted for — the reason TBR is carried as a 1.1 / 1.5 / 1.8 lever rather than a single number. Second, the burner must meet a plasma-density requirement to sustain its plug; without a demonstrated magnetic well at feasible conditions, the burner remains plug-gated. Both are stated openly on their own pages.

title: Breeder (Hyperion) Readiness Gates
lede: The specific gates the breeder must pass, from simulated plasma to a fleet that breeds net tritium.
body: From a design point to a fuel factory

The breeder (Hyperion) is a D-T spherical tokamak whose public design point is a simulated Q_sci of 3.424 at 88.7 MW of fusion power, 9.86 MA of plasma current, a 16.84 T peak field, and negative triangularity of delta -0.30. Its role is to make isotopes and neutrons — roughly a 4 kg/yr tritium class output plus about 1.97 kg/yr of helium-3 and 14 MeV neutrons — not to sell electricity. Each of those outputs sits behind a gate.
The breeding question is the crux

A breeder that cannot close its own tritium balance is not a breeder. That is why TBR is treated as a lever: 1.1 leaves little margin for losses and decay, 1.5 is a working target, and 1.8 is an aspirational upper case whose feasibility in a ported, structured machine is unproven. The local-versus-net reconciliation — breeding computed in an idealized cell versus the whole-machine balance — is an explicitly open gate.
Construction begins Q2 2027; FOAK first tritium is targeted for approximately 2030, followed by NOAK and BOAK units. No net-gain hardware claim is made before FOAK operates.

title: Burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) Readiness Gates
lede: The gates the D-3He tandem-mirror burner must pass before it can deliver resilient power on site.
body: A cleaner reaction, a harder confinement problem

The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is a D-3He tandem-mirror generator with a 26.49 T plug, a 17 T throat, a low neutron fraction of 5.44%, and direct energy conversion. Its low neutron output is what makes it attractive for fixed defense installations (Aegis) and data centers (MetroVolt). But D-3He requires far higher performance than D-T, and the tandem-mirror confinement concept must be shown to hold at feasible conditions.

In a tandem mirror, end plugs electrostatically confine the central-cell plasma. Reaching and holding the 26.49 T plug at the plasma density the design requires is unproven; without a demonstrated magnetic well at feasible beta, the burner remains plug-gated. This is stated as an open engineering-physics question, not a solved one.

D-3He also depends on a helium-3 supply, which the breeder helps provide. The burner follows the breeder in the program: it is a later test and demonstration, not a near-term deliverable, and no net-power claim is made for it today.

title: Timeline to First-of-a-Kind
lede: The dated milestones from construction start through first tritium, stated without net-gain claims.
body: The breeder program has a public timeline that is deliberately modest in its claims. Construction of the first-of-a-kind (FOAK) breeder begins in Q2 2027. FOAK first tritium is targeted for approximately 2030. Next-of-a-kind (NOAK) and balance-of-kind (BOAK) units follow, incorporating what FOAK teaches.
What each milestone does and does not mean
Construction start (Q2 2027): the machine begins to be built; it does not mean physics is demonstrated.
FOAK first tritium (~2030): the breeder produces tritium; this is the first integrated hardware result, and the earliest point any net-gain discussion is even admissible.
NOAK / BOAK: replication with learning captured — the manufacturing and integration gates mature across units.

No hardware net-gain claim is made before FOAK. The phrase "net gain 2027" has been retired from all materials; 2027 is a construction date, not a performance date. Anyone who reads a stronger claim into the timeline is reading something Kronos does not say.
The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) sits later still — a test article follows the breeder, not the other way around. Its dates are gated on the plug-density question and on helium-3 availability.

title: FOAK, NOAK, and BOAK
lede: Why the build sequence is structured so each unit retires risk for the next, and what that implies for readiness.
body: Learning is engineered into the sequence

Rather than promise a perfect first unit, the program is built around learning. FOAK (first-of-a-kind) is expected to be the hardest and most instrumented unit; NOAK (next-of-a-kind) applies the corrections FOAK reveals; BOAK (balance-of-kind) is the replicated fleet unit that benefits from a stabilized design and process.
What this means for a defense counterpart
Early units carry the most technical uncertainty and the most instrumentation; they are demonstrations, not fielded systems.
Readiness (technology, manufacturing, integration) rises across the sequence by design, not by assumption.
A capability is only as fielded as the unit delivering it — a claim about BOAK is not a claim about FOAK.

The temptation in any program is to skip ahead in the story — to describe FOAK with BOAK's confidence. Kronos does not. First tritium from FOAK, targeted for approximately 2030, is the event that starts this ladder, and each rung is claimed only when the corresponding unit earns it. This is also how manufacturing readiness matures: the fabrication route is proven on a first article before it is trusted at fleet volume.

title: What Net Gain Actually Means
lede: Scientific gain, engineering gain, and plant gain are different bars — and Kronos claims none of them in hardware yet.
body: "Net gain" is used loosely in public discussion, so it is worth being exact. Scientific gain (Q_sci) compares fusion power produced to heating power delivered to the plasma. Engineering gain (Q_eng) compares net electricity out to all electricity in, including magnets, cooling, and plant loads. Plant gain is the whole facility's balance over real duty cycles. Each bar is higher than the last.
The breeder's Q_sci of 3.424 is a simulation result, not a machine measurement.
No engineering-gain or plant-gain claim is made in hardware for either machine.
The breeder's purpose is isotopes and neutrons, so its value case does not depend on net electricity at all.
The burner targets net power but is plug-gated; a net-power claim awaits that gate.
Why the breeder sidesteps the electricity trap

Because the breeder sells tritium, helium-3, and 14 MeV neutrons rather than kilowatt-hours, its usefulness does not wait on engineering net-electric gain. That is an honest advantage: a materials-and-isotopes product can be valuable before the field solves net-electric power. It is also why the program refuses to borrow the electricity-gain narrative it has not earned.

title: Simulation vs Experiment
lede: How Kronos uses simulation, what simulation can and cannot certify, and where experiment remains indispensable.
body: Modern fusion design is impossible without high-fidelity simulation: equilibrium and stability solvers, transport models, neutronics, and magnet mechanics. Kronos uses these to close its designs and to produce the public numbers in this library. But a simulation is a hypothesis about hardware, not a substitute for it.
Explore a design space far faster and more safely than hardware.
Reproduce known experiments to earn calibrated trust (validation).
Quantify uncertainty so a result carries error bars, not just a point.
Rehearse integration and control before a machine exists.

Simulation cannot certify a phenomenon the models do not fully capture, and fusion is rich in such phenomena — edge turbulence, disruptions, materials under 14 MeV neutron flux, and tandem-mirror stability among them. A code that has never been checked against the specific regime it is used to predict is extrapolating, and extrapolation is a gate, not a guarantee.

This is why the breeder's Q_sci 3.424 and the burner's plug design are described as design & simulation studies. They are well-founded engineering predictions awaiting the only thing that can confirm them: the machines themselves, beginning with FOAK first tritium around 2030.

title: Verification and Validation
lede: Verification asks whether the code solves the equations right; validation asks whether the equations describe reality.
body: Verification and validation (V&V) are distinct disciplines that are easy to blur. Verification checks that software correctly solves the mathematics it claims to solve — via convergence studies, method-of-manufactured-solutions, and code-to-code comparison. Validation checks that the mathematics matches physical reality — via comparison to experiment. A code can be perfectly verified and completely invalid, and vice versa.
Every reported public number is reproducible from committed code and inputs before it becomes a claim.
Solvers are verified for convergence and, where possible, against analytic or manufactured solutions.
Models are validated against published experimental benchmarks from the wider fusion community.
Results are deposited with a permanent identifier so a third party can re-run them.

Kronos treats reproducibility as the minimum bar for a technical claim: a two-tier repro discipline (byte-for-byte where deterministic, tolerance-bounded where not) means an outside reviewer can obtain the same figure from the same inputs. This is what lets the program publish a physics basis openly and invite scrutiny rather than ask for trust.
V&V does not turn a simulation into a hardware result. It makes the simulation credible enough to justify building the hardware that will test it.

title: The Tritium-Breeding Gate
lede: Why tritium breeding ratio is carried as a lever, and why net breeding in real geometry is an open gate.
body: A breeder must close its own fuel loop

The breeder (Hyperion) burns deuterium and tritium; tritium does not occur naturally in useful quantity, so the machine must breed it in a lithium-bearing blanket where 14 MeV neutrons produce fresh tritium. The tritium breeding ratio (TBR) is tritium bred per tritium burned. Below 1.0 the fuel loop bleeds out; sustained operation and a surplus for products require a TBR comfortably above 1.0.
Why a lever, not a number
An idealized blanket cell can compute a high local TBR, but ports, structure, and diagnostics in a real three-dimensional machine reduce it.
Tritium is lost to radioactive decay, permeation, and processing inefficiency, so breeding must beat these before any surplus exists.
The product case (roughly 4 kg/yr tritium class) depends on net surplus after the machine feeds itself.

Kronos explicitly flags a local-versus-net TBR reconciliation as unresolved: breeding looks favorable in an idealized geometry but must be re-demonstrated once realistic ports and structure are included. Until a whole-machine net-breeding case closes — first in high-fidelity neutronics, then in FOAK hardware — the program treats robust net breeding as an open gate, not an achieved result.

title: The Plug-Density Gate
lede: The burner's tandem-mirror confinement depends on an unproven plasma-density requirement at the plug.
body: How a tandem mirror confines plasma

A tandem mirror confines a central plasma between two high-field magnetic mirrors, or plugs, that create an electrostatic potential to hold ions. The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) design specifies a 26.49 T plug and a 17 T throat. The concept's viability hinges on reaching and sustaining the plasma density the plugs require while preserving stability.
Why it is an open gate
The required plug density at feasible magnetic field and plasma beta has not been demonstrated in this design.
Tandem mirrors historically face MHD and micro-stability challenges; a demonstrated magnetic well at feasible beta is not yet in hand.
D-3He demands higher performance than D-T, so the margin for confinement shortfalls is smaller.
Without the plug, the downstream chain — burn and direct conversion — does not follow.
Stated as a requirement, not a result

Kronos flags a plug-density requirement as a caveat on the burner design point: the closing simulation reproduces on the deposited mirror, but it carries this requirement as a condition. Until the plug is shown to hold at feasible conditions, the burner is plug-gated, and no net-power claim is made for it. This is the single largest technical gate on the burner side.

title: Milestone Gating
lede: Commitments are structured so that each phase must earn evidence before the next phase proceeds.
body: Milestone gating is a decision discipline: a program does not proceed to the next phase until the current phase has produced defined evidence. Each gate has entry criteria, a body of evidence, and an explicit go/no-go. This protects a defense counterpart from a program that spends momentum instead of proof.
What a gate requires to pass
Defined, falsifiable entry and exit criteria written before the work, not after.
Evidence matched to the claim — hardware for hardware, reproducible code for simulation.
An explicit decision recorded, including no-go and rework outcomes.
No borrowing of confidence from a later phase to pass an earlier one.

Fusion programs fail slowly and expensively when phases blur together and unmet assumptions carry forward. Gating forces the open questions — net tritium breeding, the plug-density requirement, FOAK integrated operation — to be confronted at defined points rather than deferred indefinitely. The FOAK-NOAK-BOAK build sequence is itself a set of gates: each unit must operate before the next is trusted.
Milestone gating is also how Kronos keeps its public claims aligned with its evidence: a claim is upgraded only when the gate that justifies it is passed.

title: Readiness Review Process
lede: How readiness is assessed on a cadence, by whom, and against what criteria — before any external claim changes.
body: Reviews turn opinion into a record

A readiness review is a structured checkpoint that assesses whether a system meets defined criteria to advance. Reviews exist so that maturity is judged against evidence and criteria rather than enthusiasm, and so that the judgment is documented and auditable.
What a Kronos readiness review examines
Technology, manufacturing, and integration readiness together — a plant is limited by its least-ready dimension.
The status of each open gate, with evidence for any proposed change in status.
Reproducibility of the simulation results underpinning design claims.
Alignment of external materials with the current evidence — no claim ahead of its gate.

Reviews carry more weight when the reviewers are not the authors of the work. Kronos pairs internal review cadence with external scrutiny — a public physics basis, deposited reproducible results, and peer review — so that outside experts can challenge the claims. The point is not to pass reviews but to surface problems early, while they are cheap to fix.
No external readiness claim is upgraded without a corresponding review outcome behind it, which is what keeps this library's verbs honest.

title: Failure Modes and Open Questions
lede: The known ways each machine could fall short, published so partners can weigh them honestly.
body: Naming the ways this could be wrong

A credible program can state how it might fail. Below are the principal technical failure modes for each machine, drawn from the same public design basis as the rest of this library. None is hidden; each is an open question the program intends to answer with evidence.
If net tritium breeding does not close, the machine cannot fuel itself or produce surplus for products.
Centrepost and first-wall lifetime under neutron flux constrain duty cycle and availability.
Helium-3 yield depends on tritium decay handling and extraction, which is not yet demonstrated at design yield.

The plug-density requirement is the dominant risk; if it cannot be met at feasible field and beta, the tandem-mirror burner does not reach net power. Materials under even the reduced 5.44% neutron fraction still require qualification. These are the reasons the burner follows the breeder in the program and carries no near-term net-power claim.
Publishing failure modes is not pessimism; it is the precondition for a partnership built on evidence rather than persuasion.

title: The Standards Landscape
lede: A map of the codes and standards a fusion facility designs to, and how they fit together.
body: Standards encode hard-won engineering experience and give regulators, insurers, and partners a common yardstick. A fusion facility touches many standards families at once: nuclear quality assurance, pressure-boundary codes, instrumentation and control, functional safety, cybersecurity, radiation protection, and materials qualification. Kronos designs to recognized standards rather than inventing private criteria.
Quality assurance is the umbrella: it governs how every other standard is applied and documented.
Pressure and structural codes govern the physical boundary; materials standards feed them.
Functional safety and I&C govern how the plant is protected and controlled.
Cybersecurity protects the control and safety systems from digital compromise.

For a facility whose primary output is byproduct material — isotopes and neutrons — a byproduct-material regulatory framework (in the United States, an NRC Part 30 approach) is a natural fit and is being pursued through pre-application engagement. Standards and regulation are complementary: standards say how to build well, regulation says what is permitted, and both are approached openly.

title: Fusion Regulatory Framework
lede: How a fusion facility is regulated differently from a fission reactor, and the byproduct-material path Kronos pursues.
body: Fusion is not fission, and regulation is adapting

Fusion facilities differ fundamentally from fission reactors: there is no fissile fuel, no chain reaction to run away, and no long-lived spent-fuel inventory of the same kind. Regulators have been developing frameworks that reflect this lower hazard profile rather than importing fission rules wholesale.
The breeder's regulated inventory is chiefly byproduct material — tritium, activated components, and 14 MeV neutron sources.
In the United States, a byproduct-material framework (Part 30) governs such material and fits a facility whose product is isotopes and neutrons.
This framework is generally proportionate to the actual hazard, rather than reactor-scale in every respect.

Kronos pursues pre-application engagement with regulators rather than waiting for an application deadline. An earlier fusion-rulemaking comment window was missed; the program's response is to engage early and formally on the framework that applies. This library states the regulatory approach publicly and conservatively; it does not characterize any regulator's position or claim any approval that has not been granted.

Regulatory readiness is its own gate: a sound design that cannot be licensed cannot be built. Treating regulation as an engineering input from the start, not an afterthought, is part of the readiness posture.

title: IAEA and Safeguards Posture
lede: How a fusion isotope facility relates to international safeguards, and Kronos's design-for-transparency stance.
body: International safeguards, administered through the IAEA, exist to give the world confidence that nuclear materials and technologies are used for declared, peaceful purposes. Although fusion does not use fissile fuel, a facility that produces tritium and handles 14 MeV neutrons operates in a domain where transparency and accountancy matter.
Tritium inventory is tracked with material accountancy suited to a bred, consumed, and stored isotope.
Containment and surveillance are designed in, not bolted on, so inventories are verifiable.
The facility's civilian, energy-and-isotopes purpose is declared plainly and publicly.

Kronos speaks about safeguards only at the level of principle and public design intent. It does not discuss classified matters, weapons-relevant detail, or the specifics of any state's obligations. The posture is straightforward: build for transparency, keep civilian purpose primary, and make the facility's material flows accountable by design. This is consistent with the broader nonproliferation commitment described elsewhere in this category.
Safeguards readiness is treated like any other readiness dimension — designed in from the start and verified, not assumed.

title: Nuclear Quality Assurance
lede: NQA-1 and ISO 9001 govern how work is planned, controlled, and documented so quality is built in, not inspected in.
body: Quality is a system, not an inspection

Nuclear quality assurance — codified in the United States by ASME NQA-1 and complemented by ISO 9001 — is a management system ensuring that requirements are defined, work is controlled, records are kept, and problems are corrected. Its premise is that quality must be built into the process, because you cannot inspect it into a finished component.
Graded application: rigor is scaled to a component's safety and functional importance.
Design control: changes are reviewed, verified, and traced to requirements.
Records and traceability: what was built, from what materials, and how it was tested.
Corrective action: nonconformances are documented and closed, not buried.

Manufacturing readiness (whether a design can be built repeatably to spec) is meaningless without a quality system to enforce the spec. NQA-1-style discipline is what lets the FOAK breeder function as a genuine first article: deviations are captured so NOAK and BOAK can correct them. Traceability also underpins the safeguards and configuration-management posture described elsewhere.
Kronos treats quality assurance as foundational infrastructure — the umbrella under which pressure-boundary codes, I&C standards, and materials qualification are all applied and recorded.

title: ASME Pressure and Structural Codes
lede: The ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code governs the vacuum vessel, cooling, and pressure-retaining structures.
body: A fusion plant contains vacuum vessels, cooling circuits, and pressure-retaining components whose failure would be serious. The ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPVC) is the dominant standard governing the design, materials, fabrication, and inspection of such components, backed by more than a century of engineering experience.
The vacuum vessel and its penetrations, which hold the plasma boundary.
Cooling and heat-removal circuits for magnets and structures.
Tritium and fuel-system pressure boundaries requiring containment-grade integrity.
Support structures reacting large electromagnetic loads.

Designing to ASME from the outset means the structural design space is constrained by allowable stresses, qualified materials, and inspectable geometries — not by optimistic assumptions. This intersects with materials standards: a code allowable is only valid for a qualified material with known behavior under service conditions, including the neutron environment. Code compliance is part of what makes a design buildable and, later, licensable.
Kronos states code intent publicly; it does not claim certification of components that have not been built and stamped.

title: IEEE and Electrical / I&C Standards
lede: IEEE and IEC instrumentation, control, and electrical standards govern how the plant is measured, protected, and powered.
body: Measuring and commanding a fusion plant

A fusion plant is a dense instrumentation and control (I&C) problem: thousands of sensors, fast protective actions, and high-power electrical systems. IEEE and IEC standards (including IEC 61513 for nuclear I&C) govern how these systems are specified, qualified, and separated so that a fault in one does not cascade into another.
Independence and separation between control functions and safety-protection functions.
Qualification of equipment for its service environment, including radiation where relevant.
Deterministic, verifiable behavior for protective actions.
Electrical protection, grounding, and coordination for high-power systems.

The breeder's plasma control operates on microsecond timescales, coupling sensing, computation, and actuation. Standards-based I&C is what keeps such a system trustworthy: the fast control layer is engineered for determinism, and the safety-protection layer is independent of it so that a control fault cannot defeat a protective action. This separation is a functional-safety principle as much as an electrical one.

For the grid- and microgrid-facing side of the plant, interconnection standards govern how the facility connects to external power — covered separately under interoperability. Kronos designs I&C to recognized standards rather than bespoke logic, which is what makes the control system auditable.

title: ISO 9001 Quality Management
lede: ISO 9001 provides the general quality-management backbone that complements nuclear-specific assurance.
body: A general system beneath the specialized ones

ISO 9001 is the internationally recognized standard for quality-management systems across all industries. It establishes the basics — customer and requirement focus, defined processes, records, internal audit, and continual improvement — on top of which nuclear-specific assurance like NQA-1 adds its more stringent controls.
Documented processes so work is repeatable and not dependent on individuals.
Requirement traceability from customer need to delivered output.
Internal audit to find problems before an external party does.
A continual-improvement loop that turns defects into process fixes.

ISO 9001 is necessary but not sufficient for nuclear work; NQA-1 adds design control, graded rigor, and records requirements that a general standard does not mandate. Running both means the organization has a broad quality culture and the specific nuclear controls where they are needed. For a program whose credibility rests on reproducible results and honest gates, a functioning quality system is not paperwork — it is the machinery that keeps claims aligned with evidence.
Kronos describes its quality intent openly and does not claim certifications it has not obtained.

title: IEC 61508 Functional Safety
lede: Functional-safety standards define how safety-critical protective functions are engineered to a target integrity.
body: IEC 61508 (with sector standard IEC 61511) is the framework for functional safety of electrical, electronic, and programmable systems. It treats safety as a function that must be engineered to a defined Safety Integrity Level (SIL), based on the risk it guards against, and verified through the whole lifecycle from hazard analysis to operation.
Protective functions (fast shutdown, quench protection, tritium isolation) are identified and assigned integrity targets.
Safety functions are kept independent of normal control, so a control fault cannot disable protection.
Failure rates and diagnostic coverage are quantified against the SIL target, not assumed.
The whole lifecycle is documented, so integrity is auditable.

The most important functional-safety principle is separation: the systems that make the plant work and the systems that make it safe are distinct, so a single failure or a cyber compromise of control cannot also defeat safety. This principle links directly to the I&C architecture and to cybersecurity, and it is what allows a fusion plant to be operated with confidence even while its performance is still being demonstrated in early units.

title: Cybersecurity Standards
lede: IEC 62443 and NIST frameworks protect the plant's control and safety systems from digital compromise.
body: A fusion plant is a cyber-physical system

The plant's control, protection, and monitoring run on networked digital systems (operational technology, OT). Compromise of these systems is a safety and availability risk, not merely a data risk. Kronos designs to recognized cybersecurity standards — IEC 62443 for industrial automation and control, and NIST frameworks for broader risk management, including post-quantum-aware cryptography.
Segmentation into zones and conduits so a breach cannot roam the whole plant.
Least-privilege access and strong authentication for control functions.
Independence of safety-protection systems, so a cyber event on control cannot disable protection.
Continuous monitoring and an incident-response plan, not just perimeter defense.
Why this belongs in defense readiness

For a resilient sovereign-power role, the ability to keep operating under digital as well as physical stress is part of the value. A plant that provides power on a fixed installation must be defensible in the cyber domain by design. Kronos discusses this posture at the level of standards and principles only; it does not disclose specific system configurations, and it treats OT security as a first-class readiness dimension alongside physical safety.

title: Tritium-Handling Standards
lede: Tritium is a low-energy beta emitter that must be contained, accounted for, and monitored to established practice.
body: Tritium is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen that emits low-energy beta particles and is chemically hydrogen — it permeates materials and mixes into water. It is not an external-radiation hazard through skin, but it must be contained to prevent inhalation or ingestion. Handling it draws on decades of established practice at tritium facilities worldwide.
Multiple containment barriers with monitored interspaces.
Materials selected for low tritium permeability, with recovery systems on likely pathways.
Continuous air and effluent monitoring against radiation-protection limits.
Rigorous accountancy — every gram tracked — which also supports safeguards transparency.
Why it is central to the breeder

The breeder both breeds and burns tritium and produces a tritium-class product on the order of 4 kg/yr, so tritium handling is not a side system — it is core plant infrastructure. It also determines the helium-3 product, since helium-3 arises from tritium decay and must be captured. Handling readiness is therefore inseparable from the breeder's product case, and it is designed to established standards rather than improvised.

title: Radiation-Protection Standards
lede: ICRP-based dose limits and the ALARA principle govern worker and public protection at the facility.
body: Keeping dose as low as reasonably achievable

Radiation protection at a fusion facility follows internationally accepted principles, based on recommendations of the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) and implemented through national regulation. The governing idea is ALARA — keeping exposure As Low As Reasonably Achievable — layered on top of firm dose limits for workers and the public.
14 MeV neutrons during operation, requiring shielding and access control.
Activated structural materials, which decay after shutdown.
Tritium, an internal-exposure concern managed by containment and monitoring.
No fission products and no long-lived spent fuel of the fission kind.

Protection is engineered in: neutron shielding and biological shields, remote handling for activated components, ventilation and monitoring for tritium, and administrative controls on access during operation. A fusion facility's radiological profile is genuinely different from fission — the hazard is dominated by neutron activation and tritium rather than a large inventory of long-lived fission products — and the regulatory framework reflects that. Kronos states dose-management intent at the level of principle and design; it does not publish site-specific analyses in this public library.
Radiation-protection readiness is a licensing prerequisite and is treated as such from early design.

title: Materials Standards and Qualification
lede: Structural materials must be qualified for the fusion neutron environment against recognized codes and test standards.
body: Materials under an unusually harsh flux

Fusion structural materials face 14 MeV neutrons that displace atoms and generate helium and hydrogen within the metal, degrading properties over time. Qualifying materials for this environment draws on nuclear structural codes (such as RCC-MRx) and material test standards (such as ASTM methods), extended by fusion-specific irradiation data.
Reduced-activation ferritic-martensitic (RAFM) steels are the leading structural candidates, but full 14 MeV-spectrum qualification data are limited worldwide.
Neutron flux drives first-wall and centrepost lifetime, constraining duty cycle and availability.
The burner's lower neutron fraction (5.44%) eases but does not eliminate the materials challenge.
Why this is a readiness gate

A design allowable stress is only valid for a material whose behavior under service conditions is known. Because a dedicated 14 MeV fusion neutron source for materials testing is itself scarce, materials qualification is an active gate for the whole field — and one where the breeder's own 14 MeV neutrons are useful for testing. Kronos treats structural-materials lifetime as an open engineering question, stated honestly rather than assumed solved.

title: Export-Control Framework
lede: Fusion technology intersects export-control regimes; Kronos designs its disclosures to respect them by default.
body: Some knowledge is controlled for good reason

Fusion research produces knowledge, materials, and equipment that can fall under export-control regimes — in the United States, the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and, for defense articles, the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), with parallels in other jurisdictions. These regimes govern what technical data and hardware may be shared, with whom, and under what authorization.
Public materials are written to a conservative, public-only standard — physics basis and design intent, not controlled technical detail.
A firewall separates what is published from what is controlled; the two do not mix by accident.
Weapons-relevant detail is never published, regardless of framing.
Sharing of any controlled data follows applicable authorization, determined case by case with counsel.

Kronos publishes a public physics basis because credibility depends on scrutiny, and because most of the fusion physics that closes its designs is already in the open literature. What is controlled is the specific, sensitive detail — and that stays out of public channels. This library is, by design, on the public side of the firewall: it explains what the machines are and how ready they are, without disclosing anything that export control would restrict.
Export-control readiness is part of responsible dual-use posture: getting the disclosure boundary right is a precondition for any defense engagement.

title: Environmental Compliance
lede: Water use, activated-material handling, and effluent monitoring are designed to environmental standards from the start.
body: A facility cannot be built without satisfying environmental requirements — water use, effluent limits, waste classification, and site impact. Fusion's environmental profile is favorable relative to many energy sources: no carbon combustion, no fission-product inventory, and waste dominated by activated structural materials that decay over engineering timescales rather than geological ones.
Cooling-water demand and thermal management, assessed per product and housing.
Activated structural components, which are radioactive but decay and are not long-lived fission waste.
Tritium effluent to air and water, monitored against radiation-protection limits.
Solid-waste classification and handling under applicable rules.

Kronos conducts environmental screening per product (breeder and burner housings) and resolves open items internally before making any external claim; a screening that mistook scale for dirtiness was rejected precisely because it compared unlike quantities. This library does not publish site-specific environmental analyses or economics; it states that environmental compliance is treated as a design input and a licensing prerequisite, not a downstream formality.
Doing the environmental work early is part of what makes the Q2 2027 construction start credible rather than aspirational.

title: Occupational Safety
lede: Conventional and radiological worker-safety standards apply alongside the plant's nuclear-specific controls.
body: A fusion facility carries the same industrial hazards as any large plant — high voltage, cryogenics, high magnetic fields, pressurized systems, and heavy lifts — in addition to its radiological ones. Occupational safety follows established workplace standards (in the United States, OSHA-based) layered with radiation-protection controls.
Hazard analysis for each system, with controls following the hierarchy: eliminate, substitute, engineer, then administrate.
Interlocks and exclusion zones for high-field and high-voltage areas.
Training, procedures, and permit-to-work for hazardous tasks.

Occupational safety readiness is about culture as much as hardware: reporting near-misses, learning from them, and empowering workers to stop unsafe work. For a defense-facing program building first-of-a-kind hardware, a mature safety culture is also a signal of engineering discipline generally. Kronos treats worker safety as a design constraint from the beginning, integrated with functional safety and radiation protection rather than handled separately.

title: Supply-Chain Assurance
lede: A defense-grade program needs a traceable, resilient, and secure supply chain for critical components.
body: The plant is only as trustworthy as its parts

Critical components — superconducting conductor, code-stamped structures, tritium-system materials — must come from qualified sources with documented provenance. Supply-chain assurance covers three concerns at once: quality (parts meet spec), resilience (parts are available when needed), and security (parts are what they claim to be, free of tampering or counterfeits).
High-field REBCO conductor is a specialty product whose supply is maturing but not yet at fleet scale.
Nuclear-grade fabrication capacity (welding, inspection) is limited and must be qualified for these components.
Sovereign and allied sourcing matters for a defense-facing program.
Counterfeit or substituted parts are a security as well as a quality risk.

Manufacturing readiness assumes the inputs exist and are trustworthy; supply-chain assurance is what makes that assumption real. The FOAK-NOAK-BOAK sequence also matters here — early units surface supply-chain bottlenecks so they can be resolved before fleet volume. For a resilient sovereign-power role, the supply chain behind the plant must itself be resilient, which is why sourcing is treated as part of the readiness posture rather than a procurement afterthought.

title: Configuration Management
lede: Knowing exactly what was built, from what, and to which revision is fundamental to safety and to fleet replication.
body: One source of truth for the as-built machine

Configuration management (CM) is the discipline of controlling and recording the exact configuration of a system: which design revision, which components, which materials, which software version. Without it, a first-of-a-kind machine cannot be reliably reproduced, and problems cannot be traced to a cause.
Design baselines and every controlled change against them.
The as-built record: serial numbers, material certificates, test results.
Software and firmware versions in control and safety systems.
Interfaces, so a change on one side of an interface is reconciled with the other.
Why it is decisive for FOAK to BOAK

The whole learning premise of FOAK-NOAK-BOAK depends on knowing precisely what the first unit was, so that changes can be attributed and improvements carried forward. Configuration management is also a safety and security matter: an uncontrolled change can defeat a safety analysis, and an unrecorded software version can hide a vulnerability. For a defense counterpart, rigorous CM is evidence that the program can replicate a capability faithfully rather than build a series of one-offs.
CM sits under the quality-assurance umbrella and feeds directly into traceability and supply-chain assurance.

title: Documentation and Traceability
lede: Every claim traces to evidence, every component to its records — the audit trail that makes a program credible.
body: If it isn't recorded, it didn't happen

Traceability is the ability to follow any claim, component, or result back to its origin: a performance number to the code and inputs that produced it, a weld to the qualified procedure and welder, a material to its certificate. It is the connective tissue of quality assurance, configuration management, and honest technical communication.
Technical-claim chain: each public number (Q_sci 3.424, TBR levers, plug design) traces to reproducible code, inputs, and a deposited record with a permanent identifier.
Physical chain: each component traces to its material certificate, fabrication records, and test results.

This library can distinguish simulated from measured only because the underlying results are documented and reproducible. A number without a traceable origin is an assertion; a number with one is a claim a reviewer can check. Kronos deposits its results so a third party can re-run them, and it keeps records so that as the program moves from design to hardware, every upgrade in a claim is backed by an upgrade in evidence.
For defense engagement, a complete, auditable record is often as important as the capability itself — it is what allows an independent party to trust the readiness story rather than take it on faith.

title: Interoperability and Interconnection
lede: Standards for connecting to grids and microgrids let the burner deliver power to an installation predictably.
body: Power has to plug in somewhere

A generator that provides power to a base or data center must interconnect with the local electrical system — a grid, a microgrid, or an islanded installation network. Interconnection and interoperability standards (such as IEEE 1547 for distributed resources and microgrid standards) define voltage, frequency, protection, and behavior during disturbances.
Voltage and frequency ranges the source must hold and ride through.
Protection coordination so faults are cleared without cascading.
Behavior during disturbances, including islanding and reconnection.
Communication and control interfaces for dispatch and monitoring.
Why it matters for resilient power

The burner's defense value is resilient sovereign power on a fixed installation, which often means operating within a microgrid that can island from any external grid. Standards-based interconnection is what lets the generator integrate predictably with existing site infrastructure and other sources rather than requiring a bespoke electrical design at every site. This is a burner-side readiness item that follows the plug-density gate: interconnection matters only once the machine can produce net power, which remains gated.
Kronos designs to recognized interconnection standards so that, when the burner is demonstrated, integration is an engineering exercise rather than a research one.

title: Responsible Dual-Use Posture
lede: How Kronos serves defense while keeping civilian energy primary and making only conservative, public claims.
body: Fusion is inherently dual-use: the same isotopes, neutrons, and resilient power that serve civilian purposes also have defense value. Kronos does not pretend otherwise. Instead it adopts an explicit posture: civilian energy and isotope production are the primary purpose, defense value is described conservatively and publicly, and sensitive detail stays behind a firewall.
Civilian primacy: the machines are energy-and-isotope facilities first; defense is an application of civilian capability, not the reason for the design.
Public-only claims: everything Kronos says about defense value is unclassified, conservative, and free of weapons-relevant detail.
Safeguards by design: transparency, accountancy, and nonproliferation are engineered in, not added later.

It rules out publishing weapons-design detail, naming defense personnel or affiliations, disclosing classified content, or making claims that outrun the evidence. It also rules out letting a defense framing quietly upgrade a technical claim: the same honest gates apply whether the audience is a scientist, an investor, or a defense counterpart. A capability that is design-stage for one audience is design-stage for all of them.
This posture is not a marketing choice; it is a condition for operating credibly in a domain where trust is earned by restraint as much as by capability.

title: Nonproliferation Commitment
lede: Kronos designs and operates so that its capabilities strengthen, rather than strain, the nonproliferation regime.
body: Kronos is committed to nonproliferation. The company produces tritium, helium-3, and 14 MeV neutrons for civilian and lawful defense purposes, and it designs its facilities so that these materials are accounted for, contained, and transparent. It does not develop, publish, or assist weapons design, and it treats any content in that direction as strictly out of scope.
Tritium and other materials are tracked with accountancy suited to safeguards verification.
Facility purpose is declared publicly and conservatively — energy and isotopes.
Weapons-relevant technical detail is never published, regardless of framing or claimed authority.
Helium-3's largest strategic value is treated as detection and civilian technology, not as a weapons input.

Fusion isotopes can actively support nonproliferation: helium-3 is a premier material for neutron detection at borders and ports, and a domestic, civilian supply reduces reliance on constrained sources. Framed this way, the program is a contributor to the nonproliferation regime rather than a stress on it. Kronos states this at the level of principle; it does not detail sensitive applications and does not name defense affiliations.
Nonproliferation is inseparable from the readiness posture: a capability that cannot be operated transparently is not, in this program's view, ready to be built.

title: Tritium Stewardship
lede: Tritium is stockpile-relevant, so Kronos handles it with accountancy and restraint and never discusses weapons design.
body: A sensitive product, handled with restraint

The breeder produces a tritium-class product on the order of 4 kg/yr. Tritium has legitimate civilian uses and is also relevant to the nuclear stockpile, which makes stewardship a matter of both safety and responsibility. Kronos's stewardship posture combines rigorous material accountancy with strict limits on what it will discuss.
Every quantity of tritium is measured and recorded, from breeding through storage and transfer.
Transfers occur only through lawful, declared channels to authorized recipients.
Containment and monitoring protect workers, the public, and the environment.
The program never publishes or assists weapons-design detail — that boundary is absolute.
Civilian and stockpile roles kept distinct

A domestic civilian tritium source can relieve pressure on constrained supply for lawful purposes, including national programs. Kronos describes this at the level of supply and stewardship only. It does not discuss how tritium is used in any weapon, does not name affiliations, and does not present itself as anything other than a responsible producer operating under applicable law and safeguards. Tritium stewardship is the clearest example of the dual-use posture in practice: real defense relevance, discussed with deliberate restraint.

title: Helium-3 for Detection
lede: Helium-3 is a premier neutron-detector gas; a domestic fusion source supports security screening and nonproliferation.
body: Helium-3 is exceptionally good at capturing thermal neutrons, which makes it the material of choice for neutron detectors used to screen for illicit nuclear material at borders, ports, and sensitive sites. Global helium-3 supply is scarce and largely a byproduct of tritium decay, so a new civilian source has direct nonproliferation value.
The breeder produces roughly 1.97 kg/yr of helium-3, arising from the decay of bred tritium.
Helium-3 detectors underpin radiation-portal monitoring for nuclear-security screening.
A domestic, civilian supply reduces dependence on constrained legacy sources.
Helium-3 also serves quantum-computing cryogenics — a civilian demand that reinforces the case.
A capability that strengthens the regime

This is a clear instance where a fusion product supports, rather than strains, security: better and more available neutron detection improves the ability to interdict illicit material. Kronos frames helium-3's strategic value as detection and civilian technology, not as revenue and not as a weapons input. As with all products, the yield figure is a design-basis number for a machine that is not yet built; a demonstrated supply awaits the breeder's operation, and helium-3 extraction at design yield is itself an open gate.

title: Neutron-Services Safeguards
lede: 14 MeV neutron testing serves materials and detection needs under controlled, transparent, civilian terms.
body: The breeder produces 14 MeV neutrons — the fusion-spectrum neutrons that are scarce and valuable for testing how materials, electronics, and sensors behave under fusion-relevant irradiation. This is a genuine national capability gap that a fusion source can help fill, and Kronos treats access to it as something to be governed, not simply sold.
Use is for lawful, declared purposes — materials qualification, detector development, and civilian science.
Access is controlled and recorded, consistent with safeguards and export-control obligations.
Sensitive applications are handled behind the firewall, not in public materials.
Results support the field's shared materials-qualification gap, which benefits many programs.

Fusion structural-materials qualification is bottlenecked worldwide by the scarcity of 14 MeV neutron sources; the breeder's own neutrons are therefore both a product and a tool for retiring one of the field's central gates. Offering that capability responsibly — controlled, transparent, civilian-first — is part of the dual-use posture. Kronos states the capability at the level of principle; it does not disclose specific defense uses, name affiliations, or make availability claims ahead of the breeder's demonstrated operation.

title: Responsible Disclosure
lede: A deliberate split between what is published openly and what is held back keeps the program both credible and safe.
body: Credibility in fusion requires openness — a public physics basis, reproducible results, peer review. Responsibility in a dual-use domain requires restraint — no weapons detail, no sensitive specifics, no named affiliations. Responsible disclosure is the discipline of doing both at once, deciding case by case what belongs on each side of the line.
The public physics basis and design points (Q_sci 3.424, plug design, TBR levers) with reproducible results.
Honest gates, timelines, and failure modes — the readiness story in full.
Standards and compliance intent, at the level of principle.
Product roles (tritium, helium-3, neutrons, resilient power) described conservatively.

Weapons-relevant detail, classified content, controlled technical data, named defense personnel or affiliations, site-specific security configurations, and any claim that would outrun the evidence. A public/private split is maintained at the repository level — public repositories carry only public content, and confidential material is firewalled out and verified against leakage.

The two-edition discipline used across Kronos publications — a public-light edition and a confidential edition with a strict marker firewall — is the same principle applied to documents. Responsible disclosure is what lets the program invite scrutiny without creating risk, and it is a precondition for defense engagement.

title: The Classification Firewall
lede: A structural separation ensures public materials never carry classified, controlled, or weapons-relevant content.
body: A firewall, not a judgment call

The safest way to keep sensitive content out of public materials is a structural firewall rather than a case-by-case judgment made under deadline. Kronos separates public and confidential content at the source: public repositories and this library are built to carry only public, conservative material, and confidential content lives elsewhere with verification that it cannot cross over.
Confidential material is authored and stored on the private side, never in public repositories.
Automated verification checks public artifacts for markers of economics, classified, or controlled content before release.
Two-edition documents use explicit markers so a public-light edition cannot inherit confidential paragraphs.
Legal and export-control content is kept strictly out of publication and website material.

Human vigilance fails under volume and time pressure; a build-time verification step does not. This library, for example, is generated under rules that forbid economics and enforce honest gates, and the same class of check keeps classified and weapons-relevant content out. The firewall is what makes it safe to publish openly: because the boundary is structural and verified, the program can be genuinely transparent about the science and the readiness story without risking a sensitive disclosure.
For a defense counterpart, the existence of an enforced firewall is itself a readiness signal — evidence that the organization can handle sensitive information with discipline.

title: Ethics and Governance
lede: Governance structures keep the program's claims honest and its dual-use decisions accountable.
body: Honesty and responsibility do not survive on good intentions alone; they need structures. Kronos's governance is designed so that technical claims are checked against evidence, dual-use decisions are made deliberately, and no single pressure — commercial, competitive, or defense — can quietly override the standards this library describes.
Contradictions between the program's own outputs are surfaced and resolved, not silently overwritten.
External scrutiny is invited through open physics, reproducible deposits, and peer review.
Dual-use and disclosure decisions follow the firewall and export-control frameworks, with counsel where needed.
The same honest gates apply to every audience — no separate, looser story for any one of them.

The governance goal is a program that can be checked rather than one that must be believed. That means published gates, deposited results, and a record complete enough for an outside party to audit. For a defense engagement, this is essential: the counterpart is trusting not just a capability but the organization's judgment about when a claim is warranted and what may be disclosed. Governance is what makes that trust rational.
Ethics here is concrete, not abstract: keep civilian purpose primary, tell the truth about maturity, and hold the disclosure line.

title: Civilian Primacy
lede: The machines are designed as civilian energy and isotope facilities first; defense value is a derived application.
body: Both machines are conceived as civilian facilities. The breeder (Hyperion) exists to produce tritium, helium-3, and 14 MeV neutrons for civilian science, medicine, quantum computing, and energy fuel. The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) exists to produce resilient power for fixed installations and data centers. Defense value follows from these civilian capabilities; it is not a separate design.
Why primacy is more than a slogan
The designs are optimized for their civilian products, not for any weapons-relevant characteristic.
The public physics basis and reproducible results serve the civilian scientific community first.
Defense applications reuse civilian capability (isotopes, neutrons, resilient power) rather than requiring bespoke, sensitive design.
Civilian markets — quantum, medical, materials, data centers — anchor the program's purpose.
What this buys the defense counterpart

A civilian-primary program is more transparent, more scrutinized, and more broadly supported than a weapons-oriented one — which makes it a more reliable long-term partner. It also means the capabilities offered to defense are the same public, well-characterized ones offered to civilian customers, described with the same honest gates. Civilian primacy and the dual-use posture are two sides of the same coin: because the machines are civilian first, their defense value can be discussed openly and conservatively, without crossing into sensitive territory.
This is the organizing principle beneath everything else in this category.

title: Safeguards by Design
lede: Transparency, accountancy, and nonproliferation controls are engineered into the facility, not retrofitted.
body: Build it in, don't bolt it on

Retrofitting safeguards onto a finished facility is expensive and unconvincing. Kronos designs safeguards in from the start: material accountancy, containment and surveillance, and transparent declarations are treated as design requirements alongside performance and safety. This is the same philosophy as safety-by-design and security-by-design, applied to nonproliferation.
What it looks like in practice
Tritium and other material inventories are measurable by instrumentation built into the plant.
Containment interspaces and monitoring make diversion detectable, not merely prohibited.
The facility's civilian purpose is declared and its material flows are documented for verification.
The same traceability that serves quality assurance serves safeguards accountancy.

A design that is safeguards-friendly from the outset is more licensable, more partnerable, and more resilient to the trust questions any nuclear-adjacent facility faces. It also makes the nonproliferation commitment credible: the commitment is embodied in hardware and records, not just in a statement of intent. Kronos discusses safeguards-by-design at the level of principle and design intent; it does not publish sensitive specifics, consistent with the responsible-disclosure posture.
Designing for verification is, in the end, designing for trust.

title: Defense Partnership Principles
lede: The terms on which Kronos engages defense counterparts: public-first, evidence-based, and firewalled by default.
body: This category ends where a defense engagement begins: with the principles Kronos brings to the table. They are consistent with everything above — civilian primacy, honest gates, responsible disclosure — and they are stated so a counterpart knows exactly what kind of partner the program intends to be.
Public-first: engagement begins from the open physics basis and this readiness record, not from privileged claims.
Evidence-based: a capability is described at its true maturity — design-stage until a gate is passed, demonstrated only when hardware earns it.
Firewalled by default: sensitive detail is protected structurally; nothing weapons-relevant enters public channels.
Civilian primacy: the same well-characterized civilian capabilities are what defense reuses.
Nonproliferation: transparency, accountancy, and lawful channels govern every material transfer.

A counterpart can expect a program that says what it can prove, protects what must be protected, and does not let a defense framing inflate a claim. The breeder and burner are, today, design and simulation studies with construction of the first breeder beginning Q2 2027 and first tritium targeted for approximately 2030. Kronos will report progress against its published gates as evidence arrives — and only then. That restraint is the foundation on which any durable defense partnership is built.

title: Surrogates and Extrapolation Risk
lede: Fast surrogate models accelerate design but carry a specific risk: confident predictions outside their trained range.
body: Design and control at Kronos use surrogate models — fast approximations trained on high-fidelity simulations — to explore the design space and to control plasma in real time. Surrogates are powerful because they are orders of magnitude faster than first-principles solvers, but they share a well-known hazard: they can be confidently wrong outside the range of data they were trained on.
Track the applicability domain: know where the surrogate was trained and flag predictions outside it.
Attach uncertainty to every surrogate output, so extrapolation shows up as widening error bars.
Fall back to first-principles solvers for out-of-range or safety-critical decisions.
Re-validate surrogates as new high-fidelity or, eventually, hardware data arrive.
Why it belongs in the readiness story

Several headline design points involve regimes with limited direct data — D-3He burner performance and net tritium breeding among them. A surrogate that extrapolates into such a regime is making a claim the data do not support, which is exactly the kind of hidden overreach the honest-gates discipline exists to prevent. Kronos treats out-of-range surrogate predictions as hypotheses to be tested, not results, and validates against benchmarks before any number becomes a public claim.
This is the machine-learning face of the broader rule: extrapolation is a gate, not a guarantee.
